extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in computational creativity, and writers/analysts applying computational criteria to narrative/creative output
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and evaluation criteria for assessing creative outputs (especially narrative) produced by machines or humans, emphasizing novelty, value, generative capacity, and modular narrative dimensions. Useful for building, judging, or analysing computational creativity systems and their stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: generation and evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Computational creativity is 'the capacity of machines to both generate and evaluate novel outputs that would, if produced by a human, be considered creative.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both generation and evaluation are necessary: a system must produce outputs and be able to assess them (or allow assessment) for creativity; mere generation or mere evaluation alone is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fluency (Guilford)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fluency — the ability to generate many different ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure of output quantity and variety of distinct items. Note trade-off: fluent but inflexible systems produce many similar outputs (high quantity, low variety).

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility (Guilford)
rubrics_metrics.description: Flexibility — the ability to generate different kinds/kinds of ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure of conceptual diversity across outputs (different genres, approaches, or conceptual spaces). A flexible but infrequent system generates few outputs but across diverse kinds; evaluation should consider both fluency and flexibility jointly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty (necessary condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty — output deviates from the norm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty is required but not sufficient: novel output that lacks value is 'junk'. Novelty can be operationalized via similarity/statistical/information-theoretic measures or via qualitative surprise/defamiliarization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value (necessary condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Value — output has utility/quality for an audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value is required but not sufficient: valuable output lacking novelty is merely a template. Evaluation must consider audience-relevant measures of quality, usefulness, aesthetic or functional merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autonomous intentionality
rubrics_metrics.description: A creative system must have its own goals and pursue them — not merely execute external instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to fiction: characters should display intentionality (per Riedl) and systems/writers should appear to operate from inner goals or necessity rather than only following templates or prompts. Assess whether the work seems produced from internal ends rather than external choreography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual blending
rubrics_metrics.description: Creativity arises from blending elements of two unrelated mental spaces into a third novel space (Fauconnier & Turner).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate which spaces are blended, the originality of the blend, and whether the blend produces coherent, meaningful, and surprising mappings (e.g., creative metaphors, genre/plot/character blends).

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature mining / knowledge of conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems mine large textual corpora for patterns, tropes, and conventions — to know what is conventional and therefore what would be novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment should consider whether the system/author demonstrates awareness of genre conventions (derived from corpora) and whether it uses that knowledge to purposefully conform to or deviate from conventions to produce novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Models of novelty (quantitative and qualitative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative: similarity-based, statistical, information-theoretic measures. Qualitative: surprise, defamiliarization, originality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose appropriate operationalization for novelty depending on task: corpus-distance or information-theoretic scores for automated screening; human-judged surprise or defamiliarization metrics for aesthetic evaluation. Document limits of each model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation methods (human, corpus, self, hybrid)
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple proposed methods: human ratings (gold standard but expensive); comparison to a corpus (relative novelty); system self-evaluation; hybrid approaches (system filters, human final evaluation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human evaluation is authoritative but costly; corpus-based methods measure relative novelty at scale; self-evaluation can help filtering but may be biased. Hybrid pipelines often practical: automatic metrics to surface candidates, humans to judge final creativity/value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common-sense knowledge and earned violations
rubrics_metrics.description: Creative outputs must satisfy common-sense norms unless deliberately violating them; a creative metaphor is still recognizable as a metaphor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether violations of common-sense are 'earned' (meaningfully motivated) rather than accidental errors. Verify recognizability and intelligibility: readers should be able to map or infer intended meaning even when norms are bent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social creativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Creativity is not solitary: influence, dialogue, and co-creation produce more interesting outputs than isolated systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the role of social processes (collaboration, remixing, dialogic feedback) in the genesis of work; systems that enable or exploit social interaction may produce higher-quality or more original outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative kink/repair (joke diagnostic)
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrative joke contains an unexpected 'kink' or discontinuity — a surprising gap in the logic that the punchline retroactively repairs (or does not in absurdist humor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the kink/repair structure as a diagnostic for narrative surprise: measure whether the story produces a productive discontinuity that is recognized as meaningful in retrospect. This structure generalizes to many short stories (smaller, subtler versions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Story-evaluation dimensions (aggregate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories can be assessed on: fluency of the writer, flexibility of outputs, novelty of conceptual blends, value delivered to the reader, surprise plus repair structure, autonomous intentionality, and common-sense fit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit checklist for narrative assessment — apply multiple dimensions together rather than any single metric. Provide examples and justify trade-offs (e.g., high novelty with poor value vs. high value with low novelty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modularity of narrative production (Scéalability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scéalability: plotting, characterization, and rendering can be modularly engineered; the system's design constraints reveal axes of evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate stories along modular dimensions (plotting coherence, characterization depth, rendering/style quality). Analyze how modular components combine and where failures occur (e.g., strong plotting but weak rendering). Modular evaluation helps diagnose and improve system design.
